docs.title: 1.1 Introduction to General Relativity
docs.text:
Before the advent of special relativity, physics was built on classical notions of absolute space and time. When those ideas were overthrown by Einstein's special relativity, a massive task remained: reformulating physical laws to fit this new spacetime structure.

While Maxwell's theory of electromagnetism fit perfectly within the new framework (being intrinsically Lorentz invariant), Newton's theory of gravitation did not. Newton's gravity relies on the idea of an "instantaneous" influence between bodies—described by Poisson's equation \(\nabla^2 \phi = 4\pi G \rho\)—which directly violates the causal structure and finite speed of information limit set by special relativity.

Instead of simply tweaking Newton's laws to force them to fit a flat Minkowski background, Einstein sought an entirely new theory of spacetime and gravitation. His revolutionary path was motivated by two key ideas.

docs.title: 1. The Equivalence Principle: Gravity as Geometry
docs.text:
The first major realization is that all bodies are influenced by gravity, and they all fall in precisely the same way in a gravitational field. In Newtonian terms, a body's gravitational mass is precisely equal to its inertial mass (\(m_g = m_i\)).

Definition 1.1 (The Weak Equivalence Principle). The trajectory of a freely falling, uncharged test body is independent of its internal structure and composition.

Because this motion is completely independent of what the body is made of, the paths of freely falling objects define a "preferred" set of curves in spacetime. Just as inertial bodies follow straight paths in the flat spacetime of special relativity, freely falling bodies in a gravitational field follow paths called geodesics.

This led Einstein to a profound conclusion: What we perceive as a "gravitational field" isn't a separate force field at all. Instead, it is a manifestation of the curvature of spacetime—a deviation from the flat pseudo-Euclidean geometry of Minkowski space.

docs.title: 2. Mach's Principle: Matter Shapes Spacetime
docs.text:
The second motivation came from the ideas of philosopher and physicist Ernst Mach. In both pre-relativity and special relativity, the structure of spacetime is fixed; it acts as a passive, absolute stage that is completely unaffected by the material bodies within it.

Remark (Mach's Principle). The local definitions of inertia and non-acceleration should be entirely determined by the global distribution of matter in the universe, rather than an absolute background.

Einstein was deeply inspired by this philosophical stance and sought a theory where the actual geometric structure of spacetime is dynamically determined by the presence of matter.

docs.title: The Synthesis: Einstein's General Relativity
docs.text:
Einstein's resulting theory beautifully synthesizes these concepts into a coherent geometric framework:

  • Curvature equals Gravity: The intrinsic properties of spacetime are described by a metric tensor \(g_{\mu u}\) on a smooth manifold \(\mathcal{M}\). Curvature, mathematically captured by the Riemann curvature tensor, is what accounts for the physical effects we historically called gravity.
  • Matter tells Spacetime how to Curve: The curvature of spacetime is directly coupled to the stress-energy-momentum tensor \(T_{\mu u}\) (which encodes the matter and energy content) via the foundational equations of the theory.

Postulate (The Einstein Field Equations). The geometry of spacetime and the distribution of matter are dynamically coupled by the equation: $\(R_{\mu u} - rac{1}{2}R g_{\mu u} + \Lambda g_{\mu u} = rac{8\pi G}{c^4} T_{\mu u}\)$ where \(R_{\mu u}\) is the Ricci tensor and \(R\) is the scalar curvature.

In General Relativity, the fixed stage is gone. The structure of spacetime is dynamically related to the matter within it, fulfilling Mach's dream—at least in part. Thus far, this elegant theory has been in spectacular agreement with modern experiments and observations.

docs.title: What's Next?
docs.text: To truly understand General Relativity and explore its physical consequences, we must translate these conceptual ideas into rigorous mathematics. In the coming posts, we will dive into the Differential Geometry of curved spaces, exploring Manifolds, Vectors, Tensors, the Metric, Derivative Operators, and Geodesics.

docs.title: 1. Why Manifolds?
docs.text:
Our experience tells us that spacetime is a four-dimensional continuum in the sense that it requires four numbers to characterize an event. Historically, it is assumed that all events in spacetime can be put into a one-to-one continuous correspondence with the points of \(\mathbb{R}^4\).

However, in General Relativity, spacetime geometry is not a fixed background; we will be actively solving for the spacetime geometry dynamically. Therefore, we do not wish to prejudice in advance any aspects of the global topological nature of spacetime structure by restricting it to \(\mathbb{R}^4\).

Before defining the rigorous notion of a manifold, we must recall the foundational definition of an open ball in standard topology.

Definition 2.1.1 (Open Ball & Open Set). An open ball in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) of radius \(r\) centered around point \(y = (y^1, \dots, y^n)\) consists of the points \(x\) such that the Euclidean distance is strictly less than \(r\), where:

\[ |x-y| = \left[ \sum_{\mu=1}^n (x^\mu - y^\mu )^2 \right]^{1/2} \]

An open set in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is defined as any set which can be expressed as a union of open balls.

docs.title: 2. Smooth Manifolds
docs.text:
A manifold is conceptually a set made up of pieces that look locally like open subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), such that these pieces can be sewn together smoothly to form a complex global geometry.

Definition 2.1.2 (Smooth Manifold). More precisely, an \(n\)-dimensional, \(\mathcal{C}^\infty\) real manifold \(\mathcal{M}\) is a set together with a collection of subsets \(\{O_\alpha\}\) satisfying the following three properties:

  1. Each point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) lies in at least one \(O_\alpha\); i.e., the collection \(\{O_\alpha\}\) covers \(\mathcal{M}\).
  2. For each \(\alpha\), there is a one-to-one, onto map \(\psi_\alpha : O_\alpha \to U_\alpha\), where \(U_\alpha\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
  3. If any two sets \(O_\alpha\) and \(O_\beta\) overlap (\(O_\alpha \cap O_\beta \ne \emptyset\)), we can consider the transition map \(\psi_\beta \circ \psi_\alpha^{-1}\) which takes points in \(\psi_\alpha(O_\alpha \cap O_\beta)\) to points in \(\psi_\beta(O_\alpha \cap O_\beta)\). We require these subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to be open and this transition map to be smooth (\(\mathcal{C}^\infty\)).

Each map \(\psi_\alpha\) is called a chart by mathematicians or a coordinate system by physicists. For mathematical convenience, we require that the cover \(\{O_\alpha \}\) and chart family \(\{\psi_\alpha\}\) be maximal (containing all possible compatible charts).

Remark (Physical Topological Requirements). In physically realistic models of relativity, we consider manifolds which are additionally Hausdorff and paracompact.

  • Hausdorff prevents pathological "branching" spacetimes where a single particle trajectory bifurcates uncontrollably.
  • Paracompactness guarantees the existence of a partition of unity, which is strictly necessary to define integration over the curved manifold.

docs.title: 3. Product Manifolds
docs.text:
We can construct higher-dimensional spaces by combining two manifolds.

Definition 2.1.3 (Product Manifold). Given two manifolds \(\mathcal{M}\) and \(\mathcal{M}'\) of dimension \(n\) and \(n'\) respectively, we can make the product space \(\mathcal{M} \times \mathcal{M}'\) into an \((n+n')\)-dimensional manifold.

If \(\psi_\alpha : O_\alpha \to U_\alpha\) and \(\psi_\beta' : O_\beta' \to U_\beta'\) are charts, we define a new chart \(U_{\alpha \beta} : O_{\alpha \beta} \to U_{\alpha \beta} \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+n'}\) on \(\mathcal{M} \times \mathcal{M}'\) by taking \(O_{\alpha \beta} = O_\alpha \times O_\beta'\) and \(U_{\alpha \beta} = U_\alpha \times U_\beta'\). Also we can set

\[ \psi_{\alpha \beta} (p,p') = \left( \psi_\alpha(p) , \psi_\beta'(p') \right) \]

for the new product manifold \(\mathcal{M} \times \mathcal{M}'\).

docs.title: 4. Diffeomorphisms
docs.text:
We may now formally define the notion of differentiability and smoothness of maps between arbitrary manifolds, bypassing the need for any embedding space.

Definition 2.1.4 (Smooth Map & Diffeomorphism). Let \(\mathcal{M}\) and \(\mathcal{M}'\) be manifolds and let \(\{\psi_\alpha\}\) and \(\{\psi_\beta'\}\) denote their respective chart maps. A map \(f:\mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{M}'\) is said to be \(\mathcal{C}^\infty\) if for each \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), the composed map \(\psi_\beta' \circ f \circ \psi_\alpha^{-1}\) taking \(U_\alpha \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) into \(U_\beta' \subset \mathbb{R}^{n'}\) is \(\mathcal{C}^\infty\) in the standard sense used in advanced calculus.

If \(f:\mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{M}'\) is \(\mathcal{C}^\infty\), one-to-one, onto (bijective), and has a \(\mathcal{C}^\infty\) inverse, \(f\) is called a diffeomorphism and \(\mathcal{M}\) and \(\mathcal{M}'\) are said to be diffeomorphic.

Diffeomorphic manifolds have mathematically identical manifold structures; in the context of relativity, they represent the exact same physical spacetime.

docs.title: 1. Vectors in Curved Geometry
docs.text:
In pre-relativistic physics, it is assumed that space has the natural structure of a 3-dimensional vector space, once one has designated a point to serve as an origin. In special relativity, Minkowski spacetime similarly has the natural structure of a 4-dimensional vector space.

However, when one considers curved geometry, the global vector space structure is lost. There is no natural or unique notion of how to add two points on a sphere and end up on the sphere. Nevertheless, the vector space structure can be recovered locally in the limit of infinitesimal displacements about a point.

We would like to give a rigorous mathematical definition of a tangent vector at \(p\) which only refers to the intrinsic structure of the manifold \(\mathcal{M}\), completely independent of any embeddings in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), a standard vector \(v = (v^1, \dots, v^n)\) intrinsically defines the directional derivative operator \(\sum_\mu v^\mu \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial x^\mu} \right)\), and vice versa. Directional derivatives are entirely characterized by two algebraic properties: linearity and the Leibniz rule. We use this to abstract the concept of vectors.

Definition 2.2.1 (Tangent Vector). On a manifold \(\mathcal{M}\), let \(\mathcal{F}\) denote the collection of \(\mathcal{C}^\infty\) functions from \(\mathcal{M}\) into \(\mathbb{R}\). We define a tangent vector \(v\) at \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) to be a mapping \(v: \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}\) which satisfies

  • Linearity: \(v(af + bg) = a v(f) + b v(g) \quad \forall f,g \in \mathcal{F}, \ a,b \in \mathbb{R}\).
  • Leibniz rule: \(v(fg) = f(p)v(g) + g(p)v(f)\).

If \(h \in \mathcal{F}\) is a constant function, i.e., \(h(q) = c \quad \forall q \in \mathcal{M}\), then \(v(h) = 0\) because \(v(h^2) = 2cv(h)\) by the Leibniz rule, while \(v(h^2) = v(ch) = cv(h)\) by linearity. This forces \(v(h)=0\). This mathematical behavior gives a precise meaning to the concept of an infinitesimal displacement (it cannot alter a constant value).

Let \(V_p\) be the collection of all tangent vectors at \(p\). We can define addition and scalar multiplication naturally: \((v_1 + v_2)(f) = v_1(f) + v_2(f)\) and \((av)(f) = a v(f)\), meaning \(V_p\) forms a vector space.

Theorem 2.2.1 (Dimension of Tangent Space). > Let \(\mathcal{M}\) be an \(n\)-dimensional manifold. Let \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) and let \(V_p\) denote the tangent space at \(p\). Then, \(\dim V_p = n\).

Proof. > We shall show that \(\dim V_p = n\) by constructing a basis of \(V_p\), i.e., by finding \(n\) linearly independent tangent vectors which span \(V_p\).

Let \(\psi: O \to U \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) be a chart with \(p \in O\). For \(\mu = 1, \dots, n\), define an operator \(X_\mu: \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}\) by evaluating the partial derivative in the local coordinate patch

\[X_\mu(f) = \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial x^\mu} (f \circ \psi^{-1}) \right|_{\psi(p)}\]

where \((x^1, \dots, x^n)\) are the Cartesian coordinates of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). It is easily verified that \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) are linearly independent tangent vectors.

To show that they span \(V_p\), we expand \(f \circ \psi^{-1}\) around \(a = \psi(p)\) using Taylor's theorem. For all \(q \in O\) we have

\[f(q) = f(p) + \sum_{\mu=1}^n [x^\mu \circ \psi(q) - x^\mu \circ \psi(p)] H_\mu(\psi(q)).\]

where the smooth functions \(H_\mu\) satisfy \(H_\mu(\psi(p)) = X_\mu(f)\).

Let \(v \in V_p\) be an arbitrary tangent vector. We apply \(v\) to \(f\), using linearity, the Leibniz property, and the fact that \(v\) applied to a constant vanishes. Evaluating at \(p\), the terms where \(v\) acts on \(H_\mu\) zero out because the position difference \([x^\mu \circ \psi(p) - x^\mu \circ \psi(p)]\) is zero at \(p\). We obtain

\[v(f) = \sum_{\mu=1}^n [H_\mu \circ \psi(p)] v(x^\mu \circ \psi).\]

Substituting \(H_\mu \circ \psi(p) = X_\mu(f)\), we get

\[v(f) = \sum_{\mu=1}^n v^\mu X_\mu(f)\]

where the coefficients are defined as \(v^\mu = v(x^\mu \circ \psi)\).

Thus, we have successfully expressed an arbitrary tangent vector \(v\) as a linear combination of the \(X_\mu\)

\[v = \sum_{\mu=1}^n v^\mu X_\mu.\]

This shows the \(n\) vectors \(X_\mu\) span the tangent space, completing the proof that \(\dim V_p = n\). \(\blacksquare\)

The basis \(\{X_\mu \}\) constructed in the proof is called a coordinate basis. We often denote \(X_\mu\) simply as \(\partial / \partial x^\mu\).

docs.title: 2. Basis Transformation and Vector Transformation
docs.text:
By choosing a different chart \(\psi'\), we obtain a different coordinate basis \(\{X_\mu'\}\). Since \(\{X_\mu'\}\) also spans \(V_p\), we can express \(X_\mu\) in terms of the new basis \(\{X_\mu'\}\). Using the multivariable chain rule, we get

\[ X_{\mu} = \sum_{ u = 1}^n \left. rac{\partial x'^ u}{\partial x^\mu} ight|_{\psi(p)} X_{ u}' \]

where \(x'^ u\) denotes the \( u\)-th component of the transition map \(\psi' \circ \psi^{-1}\). Hence, equating \(v = \sum v^\mu X_\mu = \sum v'^ u X_ u'\), we find that components \(v'^ u\) of a vector \(v\) in the new coordinate basis are related to the components \(v^\mu\) in the old basis by

\[ v'^ u = \sum_{\mu=1}^n v^\mu rac{\partial x'^ u}{\partial x^\mu} \]

This is universally known as the vector transformation law.

docs.title: 3. Tangent of a Curve
docs.text:
A smooth curve \(C\) on a manifold \(\mathcal{M}\) is a \(\mathcal{C}^\infty\) map from \(\mathbb{R}\) into \(\mathcal{M}\) (often parameterized by \(t\) or \(\lambda\)).

At each point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) lying on the curve, we can associate a tangent vector \(T \in V_p\) with \(C\) as follows. For any \(f \in \mathcal{F}\), set \(T(f) = d(f \circ C)/dt\). Using the chain rule,

\[ T(f) = \frac{d}{dt} (f \circ C) = \sum_{\mu=1}^n \frac{\partial}{\partial x^\mu} (f \circ \psi^{-1}) \frac{dx^\mu}{dt} = \sum_{\mu=1}^n \frac{dx^\mu}{dt} X_{\mu} (f) \]

because the curve \(C\) on \(\mathcal{M}\) gets mapped into a coordinate curve \(x^\mu(t)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) when we choose a coordinate system \(\psi\). Thus, the components \(T^\mu\) of the tangent vector to the curve are simply the velocity components.

\[ T^\mu = \frac{dx^\mu}{dt} \]

Remark (The Parallel Transport Problem). We can define another tangent space \(V_q\) by choosing a different point \(q \in \mathcal{M}\). However, we do not have a natural way of identifying \(V_p\) and \(V_q\); there is no absolute way of determining whether a tangent vector at \(q\) is "the same" as a tangent vector at \(p\).

If we are given an additional structure called a connection (e.g., the Christoffel symbols), we gain a notion of parallel transport of vectors from \(p\) to \(q\) along a curve. However, if the spacetime curvature is nonzero, the identification of \(V_p\) with \(V_q\) will strictly depend on the path chosen.

A tangent field (or vector field) \(v\) on a manifold \(\mathcal{M}\) is an assignment of a tangent vector \(v|_p \in V_p\) at each point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\). Even though we do not have a notion of whether \(V_p\) and \(V_q\) are the same, we have a natural notion of \(v\) being smooth. If \(f\) is a \(\mathcal{C}^\infty\) function, then at each \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), \(v|_p(f)\) is a number, making \(v(f)\) a scalar function on \(\mathcal{M}\). The vector field \(v\) is smooth if for each smooth function \(f\), the resulting function \(v(f)\) is also smooth. In other words, a vector field \(v\) is smooth if and only if its coordinate basis components \(v^\mu\) are smooth functions of the coordinates.

We discussed that the vector space structure can be recovered in the limit of infinitesimal displacements about a point. We now show a precise meaning of this idea.

docs.title: 4. Vector Fields, Orbits, and Commutators
docs.text:
Definition 2.2.2 (One-Parameter Group of Diffeomorphisms). A one-parameter group of diffeomorphisms \(\phi_t\) is a \(\mathcal{C}^\infty\) map from \(\mathbb{R} \times \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{M}\) such that for a fixed \(t \in \mathbb{R}\), \(\phi_t : \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{M}\) is a diffeomorphism, and for all \(t,s \in \mathbb{R}\), we have the composition property \(\phi_t \circ \phi_s = \phi_{t+s}\).

For a fixed \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), \(\phi_t(p) : \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{M}\) is a curve, called an orbit of \(\phi_t\), which passes through \(p\) at \(t=0\). We can define \(v|_p\) to be the tangent to this curve at \(t=0\). Associated to a one-parameter group of transformations of \(\mathcal{M}\) is a vector field \(v\), which can conceptually be thought of as the infinitesimal generator of these global transformations.

Conversely, given a smooth vector field \(v\) on \(\mathcal{M}\), we can ask if it is possible to find integral curves of \(v\). An integral curve is a curve in \(\mathcal{M}\) having the property that one and only one curve passes through each point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), and the tangent to this curve at \(p\) is exactly \(v|_p\).

Yes, we can. If we pick a coordinate system in a neighborhood of \(p\) as in the previous proof, we see that the problem of finding such curves reduces to solving the following system of ordinary differential equations in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

\[ \frac{d x^\mu}{dt} = v^\mu (x^1, \dots, x^n) \]

By standard mathematical theorems, this system of equations has a unique solution for smooth \(v^\mu\), and thus every smooth vector field yields a unique non-intersecting family of integral curves (representing the "flow" of the vector field).

Since vector fields are essentially differential operators, they do not generally commute when applied to functions.

Definition 2.2.3 (Commutator / Lie Bracket). Given two vector fields \(v\) and \(w\), we can define a new vector field \([v,w]\).

\[[v,w](f) = v[w(f)] - w[v(f)]\]

This is called the commutator (or Lie bracket), by its action on a function \(f\).

Note that the commutator of any two coordinate basis vector fields \(X_\mu = \partial/\partial x^\mu\) and \(X_\nu = \partial/\partial x^\nu\) identically vanishes due to the symmetry of second partial derivatives. Conversely, given a collection \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) of non-vanishing vector fields which commute with each other (\([X_i, X_j] = 0\)) and are linearly independent at each point, one can always find a local chart for which they are precisely the coordinate basis vector fields.

docs.title: 2.3 Tensors; the Metric Tensor
docs.text:
Many physical quantities have a linear (or multilinear) dependence on directional displacements. For example, consider the measurement of a magnetic field. For each oriented probe (a vector), a scalar number is recorded; but there is an infinite number of possible orientations. However, we only need to test three linearly independent probe directions to know the outcome for any direction. This leads to the fundamental mathematical fact that the magnetic field acts as a linear map from vectors to scalars—precisely the definition of a dual vector.

In this section, we rigorously define vectors, dual vectors, and other quantities called tensors, which exhibit a similar multilinear dependence on multiple vectors simultaneously.

docs.title: 1. Dual Space and Double Dual Space
docs.text:
Definition 2.3.1 (Dual Space). Let \(V\) be any finite-dimensional vector space over \(\mathbb{R}\). Consider the collection \(V^*\) of all linear maps \(f : V \to \mathbb{R}\). We call \(V^*\) the dual vector space of \(V\), and elements of \(V^*\) are called dual vectors (or 1-forms).

If \(v_1, \dots, v_n\) is a basis of \(V\), we can define specific elements \(v^{1*}, \dots, v^{n*} \in V^*\) by their selective action on the basis vectors.

\[ v^{\mu*} (v_{\nu}) = \delta^\mu_\nu \]

Then, it naturally follows that \(\{v^{\mu*}\}\) forms a basis for \(V^*\), called the dual basis to the basis \(\{v_\mu\}\) of \(V\). This explicitly shows that \(\dim V = \dim V^*\). We can naturally consider the correspondence between \(v_\mu\) and \(v^{\mu*}\), which gives rise to an isomorphism between \(V\) and \(V^*\).

However, it is crucial to note that this isomorphism strictly depends on the choice of basis \(\{v_\mu\}\). Without additional structures (like a metric), there is no natural, basis-independent way of identifying \(V\) and \(V^*\).

We can push this further and consider the double dual space \(V^{**}\) of \(V\). A vector \(v^{**} \in V^{**}\) is a linear map from \(V^*\) into \(\mathbb{R}\). Interestingly, \(V^{**}\) is naturally isomorphic to the original vector space \(V\). For each vector \(v \in V\), we can simply associate the map in \(V^{**}\) whose value on any \(\omega^* \in V^*\) is purely evaluation: \(\omega^*(v)\).

So, taking a double dual yields nothing fundamentally new, and we conventionally identify \(V^{**}\) directly with the original vector space \(V\).

docs.title: 2. Tensors
docs.text:
Definition 2.3.2 (Tensor). Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space and let \(V^*\) denote its dual vector space. A tensor \(T\) of type \((k,l)\) over \(V\)

\[T : \underbrace{V^* \times \dots \times V^*}_{k \text{ times}} \times \underbrace{V \times \dots \times V}_{l \text{ times}} \to \mathbb{R}\]

is a multilinear map.

For example,

  • A tensor of type \((0,1)\) takes one vector and maps it to \(\mathbb{R}\)—this is a dual vector.
  • A tensor of type \((1,0)\) takes one dual vector and maps it to \(\mathbb{R}\)—this is an element of \(V^{**}\). However, since we identify \(V^{**}\) with \(V\), a tensor of type \((1,0)\) is nothing more than an ordinary vector.

We define the collection \(\mathcal{T}(k,l)\) of all tensors of type \((k,l)\), which possesses the structure of a vector space. Since there are \(n^{k+l}\) independent ways of filling the individual slots of a tensor of type \((k,l)\) using basis elements, the dimension of the vector space \(\mathcal{T}(k,l)\) is exactly \(n^{k+l}\).

docs.title: 3. Contraction and Outer Product
docs.text:
We now introduce two fundamental operations on tensors. The first is called a contraction with respect to the \(i\)-th dual vector slot and \(j\)-th vector slot.

Definition 2.3.3 (Contraction). The contraction is a map \(C : \mathcal{T}(k,l) o \mathcal{T}(k-1, l-1)\) defined as

\[CT = \sum_{\sigma = 1}^n T(\dots, v^{\sigma*}, \dots ; \dots, v_{\sigma}, \dots)\]

where \(\{v_\sigma\}\) is a basis of \(V\), \(\{v^{\sigma*}\}\) is its dual basis, and these are inserted into the \(i\)-th and \(j\)-th slots of \(T\). (The resulting sum is independent of the choice of basis).

The next algebraic operation on tensors is the outer product.

Definition 2.3.4 (Outer Product). Given a tensor \(T\) of type \((k,l)\) and another tensor \(T'\) of type \((k', l')\), we can construct a new tensor of type \((k+k', l+l')\) called the outer product of \(T\) and \(T'\), denoted as \(T \otimes T'\).

Given \((k+k')\) dual vectors \(v^{1*}, \dots, v^{(k+k')*}\) and \((l+l')\) vectors \(w_1, \dots, w_{l+l'}\), we define the action of \(T \otimes T'\) on these inputs as

\[(T \otimes T') = T(v^{1*}, \dots, v^{k*} ; w_1, \dots, w_l) \cdot T'(v^{(k+1)*}, \dots, v^{(k+k')*} ; w_{l+1}, \dots, w_{l+l'})\]

to be the scalar product.

One way of constructing general tensors is to take outer products of vectors and dual vectors. A tensor which can be expressed entirely as such a chained outer product is called simple. If \(\{v_\mu\}\) is a basis of \(V\) and \(\{v^{\mu*}\}\) is its dual basis, then the \(n^{k+l}\) simple tensors \(\{v_{\mu_1} \otimes \dots \otimes v_{\mu_k} \otimes v^{ u_1*} \otimes \dots \otimes v^{ u_l*}\}\) yield a complete basis for \(\mathcal{T}(k,l)\).

Thus, every tensor \(T\) of type \((k,l)\) can be expanded in components as a sum of simple tensors in this collection.

\[ T = \sum_{\mu, u = 1}^n T^{\mu_1 \dots \mu_k}{}_{ u_1 \dots u_l} \, v_{\mu_1} \otimes \dots \otimes v_{\mu_k} \otimes v^{ u_1*} \otimes \dots \otimes v^{ u_l*} \]

If \(T'\) has components \({T'}^{\mu_1' \dots \mu_{k'}'}{}_{ u_1' \dots u_{l'}'}\), then the outer product \(S = T \otimes T'\) simply has components given by the product.

\[ S^{\mu_1 \dots \mu_{k+k'}}{}_{ u_1 \dots u_{l+l'}} = T^{\mu_1 \dots \mu_k}{}_{ u_1 \dots u_l} \; {T'}^{\mu_1' \dots \mu_{k'}'}{}_{ u_1' \dots u_{l'}'} \]

docs.title: 4. Tensors on Tangent Spaces and Transformation Laws
docs.text:
So far, we've discussed tensors on an arbitrary finite-dimensional vector space \(V\). In differential geometry, we consider \(V\) as the tangent space \(V_p\) at a point \(p\) on a manifold \(\mathcal{M}\).

In this specific case,

  • The dual space \(V_p^*\) is usually called the cotangent space at \(p\), and vectors in \(V_p^*\) are called cotangent vectors (or covariant vectors).
  • We also usually refer to standard vectors in \(V_p\) historically as contravariant vectors.

We can construct a local coordinate basis \(\{\partial / \partial x^1, \dots, \partial / \partial x^n\}\) for \(V_p\). The canonically associated dual basis of \(V_p^*\) is denoted as \(\{dx^1, \dots, dx^n\}\). They satisfy the strict duality condition \(dx^\mu(\partial / \partial x^ u) = \delta^\mu_ u\).

We already showed in the previous section that under a coordinate transformation \(x o x'\), vector components transform as

\[ v'^{\mu'} = \sum_{\mu=1}^n v^\mu rac{\partial x'^{\mu'}}{\partial x^\mu}. \]

If \(\omega_\mu\) denotes the components of a dual vector \(\omega\) with respect to the dual basis \(\{dx^\mu\}\), preserving the scalar contraction \(\omega(v)\) requires them to transform inversely.

\[ \omega_{\mu'}' = \sum_{\mu=1}^n \omega_\mu rac{\partial x^\mu}{\partial x'^{\mu'}} \]

More generally, the components of a tensor in \(\mathcal{T}(k,l)\) transform by acquiring one Jacobian matrix factor for each index.

\[ T^{\prime \mu_1^\prime \dots \mu_k^\prime}{}_{ u_1^\prime \dots u_l^\prime} = \sum_{\mu, u = 1}^n T^{\mu_1 \dots \mu_k}{}_{ u_1 \dots u_l} \left( rac{\partial x^{\prime \mu_1^\prime}}{\partial x^{\mu_1}} \dots ight) \left( \dots rac{\partial x^{ u_l}}{\partial x^{\prime u_l^\prime}} ight) \]

This is universally referred to as the tensor transformation law.

docs.title: 5. Tensor Fields
docs.text:
An assignment of a tensor over \(V_p\) for each point \(p\) in the manifold \(\mathcal{M}\) is called a tensor field.

The smoothness of a contravariant vector field \(v\) was already defined earlier in the previous section. Building upon this, a covariant vector field \(\omega\) is defined to be smooth if, for every smooth vector field \(v\), the resulting scalar function \(\omega(v)\) is smooth on the manifold.

Generalizing completely, a tensor field \(T\) of type \((k,l)\) is considered smooth if, for all possible smooth covariant vector fields \(\omega^1, \dots, \omega^k\) and all smooth contravariant vector fields \(v_1, \dots, v_l\), the evaluation \(T(\omega^1, \dots, \omega^k ; v_1, \dots, v_l)\) yields a strictly smooth scalar function on \(\mathcal{M}\).

docs.title: 6. The Metric Tensor
docs.text:
Definition 2.3.5 (Metric Tensor). A metric \(g\) is a linear map from \(V_p imes V_p\) into numbers; i.e., it is a tensor field of type \((0,2)\). In addition, the metric is required to be symmetric and non-degenerate.

  • Symmetric: For all \(v_1, v_2 \in V_p\), we have \(g(v_1, v_2) = g(v_2, v_1)\).
  • Non-degenerate: \(g(v_1, v_2) = 0\) for all \(v_2\) if and only if \(v_1 = 0\).

Thus, a metric \(g\) on a manifold \(\mathcal{M}\) is a symmetric, non-degenerate tensor field of type \((0,2)\). In other words, a metric provides a (not necessarily positive-definite) inner product on the tangent space at each point.

In a coordinate basis, we may expand a metric \(g\) in terms of its matrix components \(g_{\mu u}\).

\[ g = \sum_{\mu, u} g_{\mu u} dx^\mu \otimes dx^ u \]

In physical literature, we frequently use the line element notation \(ds^2\) to represent the metric tensor

\[ ds^2 = \sum_{\mu, u} g_{\mu u} dx^\mu dx^ u \]

where the outer product sign (\(\otimes\)) is implicitly omitted for brevity.

Given a metric \(g\), we can always find an orthonormal basis \(\{v_1, \dots, v_n\}\) for the tangent space at a point; i.e., \(g(v_\mu, v_ u) = 0\) (if \(\mu e u\)) and \(g(v_\mu, v_\mu) = \pm 1\). By Sylvester's Law of Inertia, the number of basis vectors with \(+1\) and the number with \(-1\) are strictly independent of the choice of orthonormal basis. The ordered sequence of \(+\) and \(-\) signs occurring is called the signature of the metric.

Remark (Riemannian vs. Lorentzian Metrics). In standard differential geometry, we usually deal with purely positive-definite metrics (signature \(++++\)). These spaces are called Riemannian. On the other hand, the metric of spacetime in General Relativity requires a signature of \(-+++\) (or \(+---\)). Such manifolds, which possess one time-like dimension and the remainder space-like, are mathematically defined as Lorentzian manifolds.

As defined above, a metric \(g\) is fundamentally a tensor of type \((0,2)\) over \(V_p\). However, we can also view \(g\) dynamically as a linear map from \(V_p\) into \(V_p^*\) defined by \(v \mapsto g(\cdot, v)\). Because of the non-degeneracy condition, this map is strictly one-to-one and onto. Thus, we can universally use the metric \(g\) to establish a perfect, natural one-to-one correspondence between vectors and dual vectors (often referred to as "index raising and lowering").

docs.title: 1. Why Abstract Index Notation?
docs.text:
Tensors of high type are functions of many vectors and dual vectors. If we operate with these tensors, the notation becomes extremely complicated. Also, a given tensor can be viewed in a variety of equivalent ways. To solve this problem, we have introduced a basis, so that we can characterize a tensor by its components \(T^{\mu_1 \cdots \mu_k}{}_{\nu_1 \cdots \nu_l}\).

However, this component notation has a problem; if we do not specify how the basis we use is chosen, the equations we write will have a basis-independent meaning. However, in some cases, it will be convenient to use a particular type of basis, e.g., a coordinate basis adapted to the symmetries of a particular spacetime. If we do this, the equations may be valid only in this basis. It is important to make a clear distinction between equations that hold between tensors and equations for their components that hold only in a special basis. Using the component notation, this distinction is blurred.

So, we shall use a notation called the abstract index notation which is merely a slight modification of the component notation. The idea is not to introduce a basis but to use a notation for tensors that mirrors the expressions for their basis components.

docs.title: 2. Rules of Abstract Index Notation
docs.text:
The rules of the abstract index notation are as follows:

Remark (Rules of Abstract Index Notation).

  • A tensor of type \((k,l)\) will be denoted by a letter followed by \(k\) contravariant (upper) and \(l\) covariant (lower) lowercase Latin indices, e.g., \(T^{a_1 \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots b_l}\).
  • The Latin indices here should be viewed as reminders of the number and type of variables the tensor acts on, not as basis components.
  • Any lowercase Latin letters can be placed in any slot, but in any equation, the same letter must be used to represent the same slot on both sides of the equation.

For example, \(T^{abc}{}_{be}\) denotes the tensor of type \((2,1)\), obtained by contracting \(T^{abc}{}_{de}\) with respect to the second contravariant and first covariant slots.

The outer product of two tensors is denoted by simply writing them adjacent to each other and omitting the \(\otimes\) sign. Thus, \(T^{abc}{}_{de} S^f{}_g\) denotes the tensor of type \((4,3)\) obtained by taking the outer product of \(T^{abc}{}_{de}\) and \(S^f{}_g\).

Using the index notation, we can write down true tensor equations since no basis has been introduced. However, one might want to write an equation for the components of a tensor.

Remark (Component Notation Rule). Component labels in the component notation will be denoted with Greek letters.

For example, \(T^{\mu \nu \lambda}{}_{\sigma \rho}\) denotes a basis component of the abstract tensor \(T^{abc}{}_{de}\).

docs.title: 3. Advantages
docs.text:
Given any tensor equation in the index notation, the corresponding equation (with Greek \(\longleftrightarrow\) Latin replacements) holds for the basis components in any basis. Conversely, for any equation relating basis components which is a true tensor equation, the corresponding tensor equation in the index notation is valid.

The main advantage of the index notation is that one is not forced to introduce a basis unnecessarily, and one is assured that all equations written in the index notation are equations holding globally between tensors.

docs.title: 4. Exceptional Rules for the Metric Tensor
docs.text:
Some additional rules apply to the metric tensor. Since a metric tensor is a tensor of type \((0,2)\), it is denoted as \(g_{ab}\).

If we apply the metric to a vector \(v^a\), we get a dual vector \(g_{ab} v^b\). It is convenient to denote this dual vector simply as \(v_a\), thus making notationally explicit the isomorphism between \(V_p\) and \(V_p^*\).

The inverse of \(g_{ab}\) is a tensor of type \((2,0)\) and could be denoted as \((g^{-1})^{ab}\). However, we conventionally drop the inverse sign and write it as \(g^{ab}\). By definition, they satisfy

\[ g^{ab} g_{bc} = \delta^a{}_c \]

If we apply the inverse metric to a dual vector \(\omega_a\), we get a vector \(g^{ab} \omega_b\), which we simply denote as \(\omega^a\). In general, raised or lowered indices on any tensor denote the application of the metric or inverse metric to that specific slot.

For example, if \(T^{abc}{}_{de}\) is a tensor of type \((3,2)\), then \(T^a{}_b{}^{cde}\) denotes the tensor obtained via

\[ T^a{}_b{}^{cde} = g_{bf} g^{dh} g^{ej} T^{afc}{}_{hj}. \]

docs.title: 5. Symmetry of Tensors
docs.text:
The abstract index notation may also be used to neatly express the symmetry properties of tensors.

A tensor \(T_{ab}\) of type \((0,2)\) takes a pair of vectors \((v^a, w^a)\) into a scalar number \(T_{ab} v^a w^b\). We may also consider a new tensor evaluated as \(T_{ab} v^b w^a\). In the index notation, this new tensor is intuitively denoted as \(T_{ba}\). Thus, the equation \(T_{ab} = T_{ba}\) strictly says that the tensor \(T_{ab}\) is symmetric.

We can generally apply this rule to higher types of tensors. We might introduce a notation for the totally symmetric and totally antisymmetric parts of tensors.

Definition 2.4.1 (Symmetric & Antisymmetric Parts). If \(T_{ab}\) is a tensor of type \((0,2)\), we define

\[T_{(ab)} = \frac{1}{2} \left( T_{ab} + T_{ba} \right)\] \[T_{[ab]} = \frac{1}{2} \left( T_{ab} - T_{ba} \right)\]

as symmetric and antisymmetric parts of tensors.

More generally, for a tensor \(T_{a_1 \cdots a_l}\) of type \((0,l)\), we define the totally symmetric and totally antisymmetric parts over all indices as

\[ T_{(a_1 \cdots a_l)} = \frac{1}{l!} \sum_{\pi} T_{a_{\pi(1)} \cdots a_{\pi(l)}} \] \[ T_{[a_1 \cdots a_l]} = \frac{1}{l!} \sum_{\pi} \delta_{\pi} T_{a_{\pi(1)} \cdots a_{\pi(l)}} \]

where the sum is taken over all permutations \(\pi\), and \(\delta_\pi\) is \(+1\) for even permutations and \(-1\) for odd permutations.

Similar definitions apply for any isolated group of bracketed covariant or contravariant indices. For example

\[ T^{(ab)c}{}_{[de]} = \frac{1}{4} \left[ T^{abc}{}_{de} + T^{bac}{}_{de} - T^{abc}{}_{ed} - T^{bac}{}_{ed} \right] \]

Definition 2.4.2 (Differential Form). A totally antisymmetric tensor field \(T_{a_1 \cdots a_l}\) of type \((0,l)\) satisfying

\[T_{a_1 \cdots a_l} = T_{[a_1 \cdots a_l]}\]

is called a differential \(l\)-form.

If one strictly deals with differential forms, it is sometimes convenient to drop the index notation entirely and denote an \(l\)-form simply in boldface, such as \(\mathbf{T}\).

docs.title: 3.0 Overview
docs.text:
We are interested in investigating the curvature of spacetime. The spacetime manifold \(\mathcal{M}\) with spacetime metric \(g_{ab}\) is not naturally embedded in a higher-dimensional space. We wish to develop an intrinsic notion of curvature that can be applied to any manifold without reference to a higher-dimensional space in which it is embedded.

Such a notion of curvature can be elegantly defined by parallel transport. We have an intuitive notion of parallel transport on surfaces like a flat plane or a curved sphere. Then, we can alternatively characterize the curvature as follows:

Remark (Geodesics and Curvature). A geodesic is a curve whose tangent vector is parallel transported along itself. That is, it is the straightest possible curve in that geometry. A space will be considered curved if and only if some initially parallel geodesics fail to remain parallel.

However, given only the bare manifold structure of space, we do not have a natural notion of parallel transport. Given two points \(p\) and \(q\) in a manifold, their tangent spaces \(V_p\) and \(V_q\) are strictly different vector spaces, and hence there is no absolute way of saying that a vector at \(p\) is "the same" as a vector at \(q\). Thus, we need more than just the manifold structure to define parallel transport.

Knowing how to parallel transport vectors is fundamentally equivalent to knowing how to take derivatives of vector fields. If we know how to parallel transport vectors along a curve, we can define the derivative of a vector field in the direction of the curve by comparing the vectors. Conversely, given a notion of a derivative, we can define a vector to be parallel transported if its derivative along the given curve is exactly zero.

The failure of a vector to return to its original value when parallel transported around a closed loop translates mathematically into the non-commutativity of derivatives. So, the rigorous notion of curvature can be defined in terms of the failure of successive differentiations on tensor fields to commute.

Then, what extra structure do we need to define parallel transport on a manifold? Given a metric, there is a unique definition of parallel transport which strictly preserves the inner products of all pairs of vectors. So, given a manifold and a metric \((\mathcal{M} , g_{ab})\), we can uniquely define both the notion of parallel transport and the notion of derivative operators on a manifold.

docs.title: 1. Definitions
docs.text:
Definition 3.1.1 (Derivative Operator). A derivative operator \( abla\), which is sometimes called a covariant derivative on a manifold \(\mathcal{M}\), is a map which takes each smooth tensor field of type \((k,l)\) to a smooth tensor field of type \((k,l+1)\) and satisfies the five properties below:

  • Linearity: For all \(A, B \in \mathcal{T}(k, l)\) and \(\alpha, eta \in \mathbb{R}\),
\[ abla_c(\alpha A^{a_1 \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots b_l} + eta B^{a_1 \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots b_l}) = \alpha abla_c A^{a_1 \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots b_l} + eta abla_c B^{a_1 \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots b_l} \]
  • Leibniz rule: For all \(A \in \mathcal{T}(k, l)\), \(B \in \mathcal{T}(k', l')\),
\[ egin{aligned} abla_e[A^{a_1 \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots b_l} B^{c_1 \cdots c_{k'}}{}_{d_1 \cdots d_{l'}}] &= [ abla_e A^{a_1 \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots b_l}]B^{c_1 \cdots c_{k'}}{}_{d_1 \cdots d_{l'}} \ &\quad + A^{a_1 \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots b_l}[ abla_e B^{c_1 \cdots c_{k'}}{}_{d_1 \cdots d_{l'}}] \quad . \end{aligned} \]
  • Commutativity with contraction: For all \(A \in \mathcal{T}(k, l)\),
\[ abla_d(A^{a_1 \cdots c \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots c \cdots b_l}) = abla_d A^{a_1 \cdots c \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots c \cdots b_l} \]
  • Consistency with the notion of tangent vectors as directional derivatives on scalar fields: For all \(f \in \mathcal{F}\) and all \(t^a \in V_p\),
\[ t(f) = t^a abla_a f \quad . \]
  • Torsion free:1 For all \(f \in \mathcal{F}\),
\[ abla_a abla_b f = abla_b abla_a f \quad . \]

\(\;\)

If we have \(T^{a_1 \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots b_l} \in \mathcal{T}(k,l)\), we denote the tensor field resulting from the action of \( abla\) on \(T\) by \( abla_c \, T^{a_1 \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots b_l}\).

Conditions 4 and 5 with the Leibniz rule allow us to derive a simple expression for the commutator of two vector fields \(v^a\), \(w^b\) in terms of any derivative operator \( abla_a\). Applied to any smooth function \(f\),

\[ egin{aligned} [v, w](f) &= v\{w(f)\} - w\{v(f)\} \\ &= v^a abla_a (w^b abla_b f) - w^a abla_a (v^b abla_b f) \\ &= \{v^a abla_a w^b - w^a abla_a v^b\} abla_b f . \end{aligned} \]

Thus we have

\[ \left [ v , w ight ]^b = v^a abla_{a} w^b - w^a abla_{a} v^b. \]

docs.title: 2. Existence and Uniqueness of Derivative Operator
docs.text:
Now we show that derivative operators exist. Let \(\psi\) be a coordinate system and let \(\{\partial / \partial x^\mu \}\) and \(\{dx^\mu\}\) be associated coordinate bases. Then in the region covered by these coordinates, we may define a derivative operator, \(\partial_a\), called an ordinary derivative as follows.

For any smooth tensor field \(T^{a_1 \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots b_l}\) we take its components \(T^{\mu_1 \cdots \mu_k}{}_{ u_1 \cdots u_l}\) in this coordinate basis and define \(\partial_c T^{a_1 \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots b_l}\) to be the tensor whose components in this coordinate basis are the partial derivatives \(\partial (T^{\mu_1 \cdots \mu_k}{}_{ u_1 \cdots u_l}) / \partial x^\sigma\). Then, the five conditions follow from the properties of partial derivatives. Also, by equality of mixed partial derivatives, condition 5 holds for all tensor fields, not just scalar fields. Thus, given a system \(\psi\), we can construct an associated derivative operator \(\partial_a\).

What happens if we choose a different coordinate system \(\psi'\)? This will yield a different derivative operator \(\partial_a '\), that is, the components of the tensor \(\partial_c T^{a_1 \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots b_l}\) in the new coordinates will not be equal to the partial derivatives of the primed components of \(T^{a_1 \cdots a_k}{}_{b_1 \cdots b_l}\) with respect to the primed coordinates. Thus, a given ordinary derivative operator is coordinate dependent, i.e., it is not associated with the intrinsic structure of the manifold.

Now we consider the uniqueness of derivative operators. By condition 4, any two derivative operators \( abla_a\) and \( ilde{ abla}_{a}\) must agree in their action on scalar fields. We consider the difference between derivative operators in the next section.

docs.title: 3. Difference between Derivative Operators
docs.text:
To investigate their possible disagreements, let \(\omega_b\) be a dual vector field and consider the difference \( ilde{ abla}_a (f\omega_b) - abla_a (f\omega_b)\) for an arbitrary scalar field \(f\). Then,

\[ egin{aligned} ilde{ abla}_{a} (f \omega_{b}) - abla_{a} (f \omega_{b}) &= \left ( ilde{ abla}_a f ight ) \omega_b + f ilde{ abla}_a \omega_b - \left ( abla_a f ight ) \omega_b - f abla_a \omega_b \ &= f \left ( ilde{ abla}_a \omega_b - abla_a \omega_b ight ) \end{aligned} \]

At a point \(p\), \( ilde{ abla}_a \omega_b\) and \( abla_a \omega_b\) each depend on how \(\omega_b\) changes as one moves away from \(p\). However, the equation above shows that their difference depends only on the value of \(\omega_b\) at the point \(p\). To see this, suppose that \(\omega_b '\) equals \(\omega_b\) at \(p\) and show that we get the same answer if we replace \(\omega_{b}\) by \(\omega_b '\). Since \(\omega_b ' - \omega_b\) vanishes at \(p\), we can find smooth functions \(f_{(\alpha)}\) which vanish at \(p\) and smooth dual vector fields, \(\mu_b ^{(\alpha)}\) such that

\[ \omega_{b}' - \omega_{b} = \sum_{\alpha=1}^n f_{(\alpha)} \mu_{b} ^{(\alpha)}. \]

Hence,

\[ egin{aligned} ilde{ abla}_a \left ( \omega_b ' - \omega_b ight ) - abla_a \left ( \omega_b ' - \omega_b ight ) &= \sum_\alpha \left \{ ilde{ abla}_a \left ( f_{(\alpha)} \mu_b ^{(\alpha)} ight ) - abla_a \left ( f_{(\alpha)} \mu_b ^{(\alpha)} ight ) ight \} \ &= \sum_\alpha f_{(\alpha)} \left \{ ilde{ abla}_a \mu_b ^{(\alpha)} - abla_a \mu_b ^{(\alpha)} ight \} = 0 \end{aligned} \]

since each \(f_{(\alpha)} = 0\) at \(p\). Thus, we have

\[ ilde{ abla}_a \omega_b ' - abla_a \omega_b ' = ilde{ abla}_{a} \omega_b - abla_a \omega_b. \]

Thus, we have shown that \( ilde{ abla}_a - abla_a\) defines a map of dual vectors at \(p\) to tensors of type \((0,2)\) at \(p\). Then, \(\left ( ilde{ abla}_a - abla_a ight )\) defines a tensor of type \((1,2)\) at \(p\), which we denote as \(C^c {}_{ab}\). To summarize, we have shown that given any two derivative operators \( ilde{ abla}_a\) and \( abla_a\) there exists a tensor field \(C^c {}_{ab}\) such that

\[ abla_{a} \omega_{b} = ilde{ abla}_{a} \omega_{b} - C^c {}_{ab} \, \omega_{c}. \]

We have a symmetry property of \(C^c {}_{ab}\). Take \(\omega_b = abla_b f = ilde{ abla}_b f\). Then,

\[ abla_a abla_b f = ilde{ abla}_a ilde{ abla}_b f - C^c {}_{ab} abla_c f. \]

Since both \( abla_a abla_b f\) and \( ilde{ abla}_a ilde{ abla}_b f\) are symmetric in \(a\) and \(b\), \(C^c {}_{ab}\) must also have the property

\[ C^c {}_{ab} = C^c {}_{ba}. \]

For a vector field \(t^a\) and \(1\)-form field \(\omega_a\), property 4 gives that

\[ \left ( ilde{ abla}_a - abla_a ight ) \left ( \omega_b t^b ight ) = 0. \]

On the other hand, by the Leibniz rule, we have

\[ \left ( ilde{ abla}_a - abla_a ight ) \left ( \omega_b t^b ight ) = \left ( C^c {}_{ab} \omega_c ight ) t^b + \omega_b \left ( ilde{ abla}_a - abla_a ight ) t^b. \]

Substituting some indices, we get

\[ \omega_b \left [ \left ( ilde{ abla}_a - abla_a ight ) t^b + C^b {}_{ac} t^c ight ] = 0 \]

for all \(\omega_b\). This implies

\[ abla_a t^b = ilde{ abla}_a t^b + C^b {}_{ac} t^c. \]

In a similar manner, we can derive the general formula for the action of \( abla_a\) on an arbitrary tensor field in terms of \( ilde{ abla}_a\) and \(C^c {}_{ab}\). For \(T \in \mathcal{T}(k,l)\), we find

\[ abla_a T^{b_1 \cdots b_k} {}_{c_1 \cdots c_l} = ilde{ abla}_a T^{b_1 \cdots b_k} {}_{c_1 \cdots c_l} + \sum_i C^{b_i} {}_{ad} T^{b_1 \cdots d \cdots b_k}{}_{c_1 \cdots c_l} - \sum_j C^d {}_{ac_j} T^{b_1 \cdots b_l}{}_{c_1 \cdots d \cdots c_l}. ag{*} \]

Thus, the difference between the two derivative operators \( abla_a\) and \( ilde{ abla}_a\) is characterized by the tensor field \(C^c {}_{ab}\).

Conversely, it is easy to check that if \( ilde{ abla}_a\) is a derivative operator and \(C^c {}_{ab}\) is an arbitrary smooth tensor field which is symmetric in its lower indices, then \( abla_a\) defined by \((*)\) will also be a derivative operator. So, on an \(n\)-dimensional manifold, \(C^c {}_{ab}\) has \(n^2 (n+1)/2\) independent components to be specified at each point.

docs.title: 4. Christoffel Symbol
docs.text:
Definition 3.1.2 (Christoffel Symbol). The important application of \((*)\) is when \( ilde{ abla}_a\) is an ordinary derivative operator \(\partial_a\). In this case, the tensor field \(C^c {}_{ab}\) is denoted as \(\Gamma^c {}_{ab}\) and called a Christoffel symbol.

For example, we write

\[ abla_a t^b = \partial_a t^b + \Gamma^b {}_{ac} t^c. \]

Since we already know how to take \(\partial_a\), we only need to know about \(\Gamma^b {}_{ac}\) to know how to compute the derivative \( abla_a\). Note that we have used a coordinate system to define \(\partial_a\). So, if we change coordinates, we also change our ordinary derivative operator \(\partial_a\) to \(\partial_a '\), and thus we have our tensor \(\Gamma^c {}_{ab}\) transformed to a new tensor \({\Gamma '}^c {}_{ab}\). Hence, the components of \(\Gamma^c {}_{ab}\) will not be related to the components of \({\Gamma'}^c {}_{ab}\) in the primed coordinates by the tensor transformation law.

We learn how to calculate the Christoffel symbols in the next few sections.

docs.title: 5. Parallel Transport
docs.text:
Definition 3.1.3 (Parallel Transport & Connection). Given a derivative operator \( abla_a\), we can define the notion of parallel transport of a vector along a curve \(C\) with a tangent \(t^a\). A vector \(v^a\) given at each point on the curve is said to be parallelly transported as one moves along the curve if the equation

\[ t^a abla_{a} v^b = 0 \]

is satisfied along the curve.

More generally, one can define the parallel transport of a tensor by

\[ t^a abla_a T^{b_1 \cdots b_k}{}_{c_1 \cdots c_l} = 0. \]

Choosing a coordinate system, we can express this as the following:

\[ t^a \partial_a v^b + t^a \Gamma^b {}_{ac} v^c = 0 \]

Or, equivalently, in terms of components in the coordinate basis and the parameter \(t\) along the curve,

\[ rac{dv^ u}{dt} + \sum_{\mu , u} t^\mu \Gamma^ u {}_{\mu \lambda} v^\lambda = 0. \]

So, the parallel transport of \(v^a\) depends only on the values of \(v^a\) on the curve, so we may consider the parallel transport properties of vectors defined only along the curve as opposed to vector fields. Also, by the uniqueness of solution of ODE with a given initial value of \(v^a\), a vector at a point \(p\) on the curve uniquely defines a parallel transported vector everywhere else on the curve.

Now, we may use this notion of parallel transport to identify the tangent spaces \(V_p\) and \(V_q\) of points \(p\) and \(q\) if we are given a derivative operator and a curve connecting \(p\) and \(q\). The mathematical structure arising from such a curve dependent identification of the tangent spaces of different points is called a connection. Conversely, one could start with the general notion of a connection and use it to define the notion of derivative operator.

docs.title: 6. Parallel Transport with Metric
docs.text:
Given only the manifold structure, many distinct derivative operators are possible and no one of them is naturally preferred over the others. We should now give a metric \(g_{ab}\) on the manifold. Then, there is a natural choice of derivative operator, which is uniquely picked out. This is because the metric gives rise to a natural condition which we may impose on the notion of parallel transport.

Given two vectors \(v^a\) and \(w^a\), we would like to require that their inner product \(g_{ab} v^a w^b\) remain unchanged if we parallel transport them along any curve. Thus, we require

\[ t^a abla_{a} \left (g_{bc} v^b w^c ight ) = 0 \]

for \(v^b\) and \(w^c\) which satisfy \(t^a abla_a v^b = 0\) which was introduced earlier. Using the Leibniz rule,

\[ t^a v^b w^c abla_a g_{bc} = 0. \]

This equation holds for all curves and parallelly transported vectors if and only if

\[ abla_{a} g_{bc} = 0 \]

which is the additional condition we want to impose on \( abla_a\). Then, this equation uniquely determines \( abla_a\) by the following theorem.

Theorem 3.1.1. Let \(g_{ab}\) be a metric. Then there exists a unique derivative operator \( abla_a\) satisfying \( abla_a g_{bc} = 0\).

Proof. Let \( ilde{ abla}_a\) be any derivative operator. We would like to solve for \(C^c {}_{ab}\) so that the derivative operator determined by \( ilde{ abla}_a\) and \(C^c {}_{ab}\) will satisfy the required property. We will prove the theorem by showing that a unique solution for \(C^c {}_{ab}\) exists. By \((*)\), \(C^c {}_{ab}\) must satisfy

\[ 0 = abla_a g_{bc} = ilde{ abla}_a g_{bc} - C^d {}_{ab} g_{dc} - C^d {}_{ac} g_{bd} \]

that is,

\[ C_{cab} + C_{bac} = ilde{ abla}_a g_{bc}. \]

Then, by substituting the indices, we also have

\[ egin{aligned} C_{cba} + C_{abc} &= ilde{ abla}_b g_{ac} \ C_{bca} + C_{acb} &= ilde{ abla}_c g_{ab}. \end{aligned} \]

By the three equations above,

\[ 2C_{cab} = ilde{ abla}_a g_{bc} + ilde{ abla}_b g_{ac} - ilde{ abla}_c g_{ab} \]

which is equivalent to

\[ C^c {}_{ab} = rac{1}{2} g^{cd} \left \{ ilde{ abla}_a g_{bd} + ilde{ abla}_b g_{ad} - ilde{ abla}_d g_{ab} ight \}. ag{**} \]

This choice of \(C^c {}_{ab}\) solves \( abla_a g_{bc} = 0\) and is unique, which completes the proof. \( lacksquare\)

Thus, a metric \(g_{ab}\) naturally determines a derivative operator \( abla_a\). For the remainder of these articles, when a metric is present, we will always choose the derivative operator to be this natural one. Furthermore, \((*)\) and \((**)\) will tell us how to compute \( abla_a\) in terms of any other derivative operator \( ilde{ abla}_a\). In particular, in terms of an ordinary derivative operator, the Christoffel symbol is

\[ \Gamma^c {}_{ab} = rac{1}{2} g^{cd} \left \{\partial_a g_{bd} + \partial_b g_{ad} - \partial_d g_{ab} ight \} \]

and thus the coordinate basis components of the Christoffel symbol are

\[ \Gamma^ ho {}_{\mu u} = rac{1}{2} \sum_\sigma g^{ ho \sigma} \left \{ rac{\partial g_{ u \sigma}}{\partial x^\mu} + rac{\partial g_{\mu \sigma}}{\partial x^ u} - rac{\partial g_{\mu u}}{\partial x^\sigma} ight \}. \]

Therefore, we can compute \(\Gamma^c {}_{ab}\) by taking partial derivatives of the coordinate basis components of the metric, and hence we can also compute \( abla_a\).

  1. If this condition is not imposed, it can be shown that there must exist a tensor \(T^c {}_{ab}\) antisymmetric in \(a\) and \(b\) such that \( abla_a abla_b f - abla_b abla_a f = - T^c {}_{ab} abla_c f\). \(T^c {}_{ab}\) is called the torsion tensor, and thus this condition states that the torsion tensor vanishes. ↩

docs.title: 3.2 Curvature
docs.text:
In flat spaces, parallel transport is trivial: a vector remains exactly the same no matter what path you take from \(p\) to \(q\). However, in a general manifold, parallel transport is intrinsically path-dependent. If we take a vector at \(p\) and parallel transport it around a closed loop, it will not necessarily return to its original orientation. This phenomenon—often called holonomy in differential geometry—is the purest geometric manifestation of curvature.

In this article, we will mathematically formalize this path dependency.

docs.title: 1. The Riemann Curvature Tensor
docs.text:
How do we measure path dependency locally, without having to integrate around macroscopic loops? We look at the failure of derivatives to commute.

If you are familiar with gauge theories in Quantum Field Theory, this concept is identical: the commutator of gauge covariant derivatives yields the field strength tensor \(F_{\mu u}\). In General Relativity, the commutator of our spacetime covariant derivatives will yield the curvature of spacetime itself.

Let \( abla_a\) be a derivative operator. Let \(\omega_a\) be a dual vector field and \(f\) be a smooth scalar function. If we apply two successive covariant derivatives to \(f\omega_a\), we get:

\[ egin{aligned} abla_a abla_b \left ( f \omega_c ight ) &= abla_a \left ( \omega_c abla_b f + f abla_b \omega_c ight ) \ &= \left ( abla_a abla_b f ight ) \omega_c + abla_b f abla_a \omega_c + abla_a f abla_b \omega_c + f abla_a abla_b \omega_c. \end{aligned} \]

Reversing the order of differentiation to find \( abla_b abla_a \left ( f \omega_c ight )\) and subtracting the two yields the commutator:

\[ \left ( abla_a abla_b - abla_b abla_a ight ) \left ( f \omega_c ight ) = f \left ( abla_a abla_b - abla_b abla_a ight ) \omega_c. \]

Notice something remarkable here: all the derivatives acting on \(f\) have perfectly canceled out. The resulting operator \(\left ( abla_a abla_b - abla_b abla_a ight )\) acting on \(\omega_c\) depends only on the value of \(\omega_c\) at that specific point \(p\), not on its derivatives. Mathematically, this means the commutator acts purely algebraically, defining a linear map from dual vectors to type \((0,3)\) tensors.

Definition 3.2.1 (Riemann Curvature Tensor). Because the commutator acts as a purely local linear map, there must exist a unique tensor field \(R_{abc}{}^{d}\) of type \((1,3)\) such that for any dual vector field \(\omega_c\):

\[ abla_a abla_b \omega_c - abla_b abla_a \omega_c = R_{abc} {}^d \omega_d. ag{*} \]

This tensor \(R_{abc} {}^d\) is the Riemann curvature tensor, encoding all intrinsic curvature of the manifold.

docs.title: 2. Quantifying Path Dependency (Holonomy)
docs.text:
To prove that the Riemann tensor actually governs the macroscopic holonomy (the rotation of a vector transported around a loop), let's construct a small closed loop at \(p \in \mathcal{M}\).

Choose a \(2\)-dimensional surface \(S\) through \(p\) with coordinates \(t\) and \(s\). We form a loop by moving \(\Delta t\) along the \(s=0\) curve, moving \(\Delta s\) along the \(t= \Delta t\) curve, and then tracing our steps back.

Let \(v^a\) be an arbitrary vector at \(p\). We want to compute the total change \(\delta (v^a \omega_a)\) after parallel transporting \(v^a\) around this loop. Let \(T^b\) and \(S^c\) be the coordinate tangent vectors to the \(t\) and \(s\) curves, respectively.

For the first leg (moving by \(\Delta t\)), the change \(\delta_1\) evaluated at the midpoint is:

\[ \delta_1 = \left . \Delta t rac{\partial}{\partial t} (v^a \omega_a ) ight \vert _{(\Delta t/2, 0)} = \left . \Delta t v^a T^b abla_b \omega_a ight \vert_{(\Delta t / 2 , 0)} \]

where we used the parallel transport condition \(T^b abla_b v^a = 0\). When we combine the forward leg (\(\delta_1\)) and the backward leg (\(\delta_3\)), we get:

\[ \delta_{1} + \delta_3 = \Delta t \left \{ \left . v^a T^b abla_b \omega_a ight \vert_{(\Delta t / 2 , 0)} - \left . v^a T^b abla_b \omega_a ight \vert_{(\Delta t / 2 , \Delta s)} ight \} \]

As \(\Delta s o 0\), this difference vanishes. This tells us a crucial geometric fact: parallel transport is strictly path-independent at the first-order approximation. Curvature is fundamentally a second-order effect.

To capture the second-order effect, we evaluate how the quantity \(T^b abla_b \omega_a\) shifts as we move along \(s\) by \(\Delta s\). This shift is dictated by the derivative along \(S^c\). Taking care to parallel transport the vectors properly, the combined change becomes:

\[ \delta_1 + \delta_3 = - \Delta t \Delta s v^a S^c abla_c (T^b abla_b \omega_a) \]

Adding the equivalent contributions from the other two legs (\(\delta_2\) and \(\delta_4\)), the total accumulated change around the entire loop is:

\[ egin{aligned} \delta (v^a \omega_a ) &= \Delta t \Delta s v^a \left \{T^c abla_c (S^b abla_b \omega_a) - S^c abla_c (T^b abla_b \omega_a ) ight \} \ &= \Delta t \Delta s v^a T^c S^b ( abla_c abla_b - abla_b abla_c) \omega_a \ &= \Delta t \Delta s v^a T^c S^b R_{cba}{}^{d} \omega_d \end{aligned} \]

(Note that we used the fact that coordinate bases commute, \([T, S] = 0\), to combine the derivatives). Stripping away the arbitrary dual vector \(\omega_a\), the actual physical vector \(v^a\) experiences a shift of:

\[ \delta v^a = \Delta t \Delta s v^d T^c S^b R_{cbd}{}^a. \]

This elegantly confirms our intuition: the Riemann tensor is exactly the machine that takes in the area of a loop (\(T^c S^b\)) and an initial vector (\(v^d\)), and spits out the discrepancy (\(\delta v^a\)) caused by traversing that loop.

docs.title: 3. Algebraic Properties of the Riemann Tensor
docs.text:
Using equation \((*)\), we can generalize the commutator action to arbitrary tensor fields. For instance, applying it to a vector field \(t^c\) yields:

\[ \left ( abla_a abla_b - abla_b abla_a ight ) t^c = - R_{abd}{}^c t^d. \]

By induction, this pattern extends to any tensor \(T^{c_1 \cdots c_k}{}_{d_1 \cdots d_l}\) by adding one Riemann term for every upper index and subtracting one for every lower index:

\[ \left ( abla_a abla_b - abla_b abla_a ight ) T^{c_1 \cdots c_k}_{d_1 \cdots d_l} = - \sum_{i=1}^{k} R_{abe}{}^{c_i} T^{c_1 \cdots e \cdots c_k}{}_{d_1 \cdots d_l} + \sum_{j=1}^{l} R_{abd_j} {}^{e} T^{c_1 \cdots c_k}{}_{d_1 \cdots e \cdots d_l}. \]

The Riemann tensor possesses several strict symmetries, greatly reducing its number of independent components:

  1. Antisymmetry in the first pair: \(R_{abc}{}^d = - R_{bac}{}^d\)

  2. Cyclic identity: \(R_{[abc]}{}^{d} = 0\)

  3. For a metric-compatible derivative (\( abla_a g_{bc} = 0\)), raising/lowering indices reveals antisymmetry in the second pair:

\[ R_{abcd} = - R_{abdc}. \]
  1. The Bianchi identity, which acts as the geometric equivalent of the homogeneous Maxwell equations (\(dF = 0\)), dictates that the differential behavior of curvature is highly constrained:
\[ abla_{[a} R_{bc]d}{}^e = rac{1}{6} \left( abla_a R_{bcd}{}^e + abla_b R_{cad}{}^e + abla_c R_{abd}{}^e - abla_a R_{cbd}{}^e - abla_b R_{acd}{}^e - abla_c R_{bad}{}^e ight) = 0. \]

docs.title: 4. Decomposing Curvature: Trace and Trace-Free Parts
docs.text:
From a group theory perspective, we often want to break tensors down into their irreducible representations. For the Riemann tensor, this means separating it into its trace and trace-free components.

Because of its antisymmetry, taking the trace over the first two or last two indices yields zero. However, tracing over the first and third indices extracts a highly non-trivial symmetric tensor.

Definition 3.2.2 (Ricci Tensor and Scalar Curvature). The trace of the Riemann tensor over its first and third indices defines the Ricci tensor \(R_{ac}\):

\[ R_{ac} = R_{abc}{}^{b}. \]

Taking the trace one step further yields a single invariant number, the scalar curvature \(R\):

\[ R = R_{a}{}^a. \]

Physically, the Ricci tensor measures how volumes deform as they move through curved space. Due to the block symmetries of the Riemann tensor (\(R_{abcd} = R_{cdab}\)), the Ricci tensor is strictly symmetric: \(R_{ac} = R_{ca}\).

What about the "leftover" curvature that doesn't change volume, but rather shears and stretches it (like tidal forces)? That is captured by the trace-free part.

Definition 3.2.3 (Weyl Tensor). For manifolds of dimension \(n \ge 3\), the completely trace-free part of the curvature is the Weyl tensor, \(C_{abcd}\), defined by:

\[ R_{abcd} = C_{abcd} + \frac{2}{n-2} \left ( g_{a[c}R_{d]b} - g_{b[c}R_{d]a} \right ) - \frac{2}{(n-1)(n-2)} R g_{a[c} g_{d]b}. \]

The Weyl tensor inherits all the algebraic symmetries (1, 2, and 3) of the Riemann tensor but has exactly zero trace in any pair of indices. Most profoundly, the Weyl tensor is entirely invariant under conformal transformations (\(g_{ab} \to \Omega^2 g_{ab}\)), which is why it is often referred to as the conformal tensor.

docs.title: 5. The Einstein Tensor
docs.text:
The Bianchi identity isn't just a geometric curiosity; it is the mathematical foundation for Einstein's field equations. If we contract the Bianchi identity twice, we find a profound conservation law.

First, contract over \(a\) and \(e\):

\[ abla_a R_{bcd}{}^a + abla_b R_{cd} - abla_c R_{bd} = 0. \]

Next, raise the index \(d\) with the inverse metric and contract over \(b\) and \(d\). The result simplifies beautifully to:

\[ abla_a R_{c}{}^a + abla_b R_c {}^b - abla_c R = 0 \]

which can be factored into a strictly divergence-free expression:

\[ abla^a G_{ab} = 0 \]

Definition 3.2.4 (Einstein Tensor). The geometrically conserved quantity derived from the contracted Bianchi identity is the Einstein tensor, defined as:

\[ G_{ab} = R_{ab} - rac{1}{2} R g_{ab}. \]

Because \( abla^a G_{ab} = 0\) is a strict mathematical identity, \(G_{ab}\) is the perfect geometric counterpart to couple to the stress-energy tensor \(T_{ab}\), which is also conserved (\( abla^a T_{ab} = 0\)) due to Noether's theorem and translation symmetry.

docs.title: Part 3: Geodesics and Manifold Curvature
docs.text: Continuing our rigorous progression through the foundations of General Relativity, we now turn our attention to geodesics. In flat space, straight lines are trivial, but on a general curved manifold, we must fundamentally redefine what it means for a curve to be "straight." By leveraging our previously defined derivative operator, we can construct coordinate systems uniquely adapted to the manifold's geometry and explicitly relate the behavior of these curves to the Riemann curvature tensor.

docs.title: 1. The Geodesic Equation
docs.text:
Intuitively, geodesics are lines that curve as little as possible—the straightest possible lines in a given geometry.

Definition 3.3.1 (Geodesic). Given a derivative operator \( abla_a\), a geodesic is a curve whose tangent vector is parallel propagated along itself. That is, a curve whose tangent \(T^a\) satisfies:

\[T^a abla_{a} T^b = 0\]

To satisfy the purely geometric requirement that the curve be as straight as possible, we technically only require that the tangent vector point in the same direction as itself when parallel propagated. This yields a weaker condition:

\[T^a abla_a T^b = \alpha T^b\]

where \(\alpha\) is an arbitrary function along the curve. However, we can always reparameterize the curve to eliminate \(\alpha\) and recover the strict zero condition. A parameterization that satisfies \(T^a abla_a T^b = 0\) is called an affine parameterization.

Let \(\psi\) be a coordinate system mapping the geodesic into a curve \(x^\mu (t)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The components \(T^\mu\) of \(T^a\) must satisfy:

\[ rac{dT^\mu}{dt} + \sum_{\sigma , u} \Gamma^{\mu}{}_{\sigma u} T^\sigma T^ u = 0\]

Substituting the explicit definition of the tangent vector \(T^\mu = dx^\mu / dt\), we obtain the geodesic equation in a coordinate basis:

\[ rac{d^2 x^\mu}{dt^2} + \sum_{\sigma , u} \Gamma^\mu{}_{\sigma u} rac{dx^\sigma}{dt} rac{dx^ u}{dt} = 0\]

This represents a coupled system of \(n\) second-order ordinary differential equations. By standard existence and uniqueness theorems for ODEs, this system always has a unique solution for any given initial position \(x^\mu\) and initial velocity \(dx^\mu / dt\). Thus, given any point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) and any initial tangent vector \(T^a \in V_p\), there exists a unique geodesic through \(p\) with tangent \(T^a\).

docs.title: 2. Exponential Map and Riemannian Normal Coordinates
docs.text:
The existence and uniqueness of geodesics provide a powerful tool for constructing coordinate systems that drastically simplify local computations.

Definition 3.3.2 (Exponential Map). Let \(p \in \mathcal{M}\). The exponential map is a map from the tangent space \(V_p\) to the manifold \(\mathcal{M}\). It maps a tangent vector \(T^a \in V_p\) to the point in \(\mathcal{M}\) that lies at a unit affine parameter (\(t=1\)) from \(p\) along the unique geodesic passing through \(p\) with initial tangent \(T^a\).

While geodesics may eventually cross or encounter singularities, there always exists a sufficiently small neighborhood of the origin in \(V_p\) where the exponential map is strictly well-defined and one-to-one.

Because \(V_p\) is an \(n\)-dimensional vector space, it is naturally isomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^n\). By using the exponential map to project the Cartesian coordinates of the tangent space directly onto the manifold \(\mathcal{M}\), we construct Riemannian normal coordinates at \(p\).

This coordinate system has two defining structural advantages: * All geodesics passing through \(p\) are mapped into perfectly straight lines passing through the origin of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). * The connection coefficients (Christoffel symbols), \(\Gamma^\mu_{\sigma\nu}\), strictly vanish at the point \(p\), vastly simplifying local tensor calculus.

docs.title: 3. Gaussian Normal Coordinates (Synchronous Coordinates)
docs.text:
While Riemannian normal coordinates provide a local flattening around a single point \(p\), we often need coordinate systems adapted to the time evolution of spacetime, such as in cosmological models or the \((3+1)\) ADM decomposition.

When our calculations involve an \((n-1)\)-dimensional embedded submanifold (a hypersurface \(S\)), we utilize Gaussian normal coordinates (or synchronous coordinates).

At each point \(p \in S\), the tangent space of the hypersurface can be viewed as an \((n-1)\)-dimensional subspace of the full tangent space \(V_p\) of \(\mathcal{M}\). Consequently, there exists a unique normal vector \(n^a \in V_p\) that is strictly orthogonal to all vectors in the tangent space of \(S\) (with respect to the metric \(g_{ab}\)). If \(S\) is a non-null hypersurface, we normalize \(n^a\) such that \(g_{ab}n^a n^b = \pm 1\).

We construct Gaussian normal coordinates as follows:

  1. For every point \(p \in S\), construct the unique geodesic through \(p\) with the initial tangent vector \(n^a\).
  2. Choose arbitrary coordinates \((x^1, \dots, x^{n-1})\) on a domain of the hypersurface \(S\).
  3. Label each point in the neighborhood of \(S\) by the affine parameter \(t\) along its corresponding geodesic, and the coordinates \((x^1, \dots, x^{n-1})\) of its origin point \(p \in S\).

This yields the coordinate chart \(q \mapsto (x^1, \dots, x^{n-1}, t)\). A crucial geometric property of Gaussian normal coordinates is that the geodesics remain orthogonal to all hypersurfaces \(S_t\) defined by \(t = ext{Const}\).

Proof of Preserved Orthogonality. By construction, orthogonality holds on \(S_0 = S\). We must prove that the geodesic tangent field \(n^a\) remains orthogonal to the coordinate basis fields \(X_1^a, \dots, X_{n-1}^a\) generating the tangent space of \(S_t\) everywhere. Denoting any one of these fields as \(X^a\):

\[ egin{aligned} n^b abla_b \left(n_a X^a ight) &= n_a n^b abla_b X^a \ &= n_a X^b abla_b n^a \ &= rac{1}{2} X^b abla_b \left(n^a n_a ight) \ &= 0 \end{aligned}\]

The first equality applies the geodesic equation (\(n^b abla_b n_a = 0\)). The second equality relies on the fact that \(n^a\) and \(X^b\), as elements of a coordinate basis, commute (\([n, X]=0 \implies n^b abla_b X^a = X^b abla_b n^a\)). The third uses the Leibniz rule. The final equality holds because the normalization \(n^a n_a = \pm 1\) is constant on \(\mathcal{M}\). Since \(n_a X^a = 0\) initially on \(S\), its derivative along the geodesic is zero, proving it remains zero everywhere. \( lacksquare\)

docs.title: 4. Variational Principles: Extremizing Length and Proper Time
docs.text:
A profound property of geodesics derived from a metric-compatible connection is that they extremize the length (or proper time) of curves connecting two points.

For a smooth curve \(C\) with a Riemannian metric \(g_{ab}\), the length \(l\) is:

\[l = \int_a^b \left( g_{ab} T^a T^b \right)^{1/2} dt\]

where \(T^a\) is the tangent to \(C\). Length is invariant under reparameterization \(s = s(t)\):

\[l' = \int_a^b \left[ g_{ab} S^a S^b \right]^{1/2} ds = \int_a^b \left[ g_{ab} T^a T^b \right]^{1/2} \frac{dt}{ds} ds = l\]

For a metric of Lorentz signature \((-++\cdots+)\), we classify curves by the norm of their tangent:

  • Timelike: \(g_{ab} T^a T^b < 0\)
  • Null: \(g_{ab} T^a T^b = 0\)
  • Spacelike: \(g_{ab} T^a T^b > 0\)

For timelike curves, we extremize the proper time \(\tau\):

\[\tau = \int_a^b \left( -g_{ab} T^a T^b \right)^{1/2} dt\]

We wish to derive the condition that extremizes this functional. Focusing on spacelike curves (the timelike derivation is identical up to a sign), we treat this as a Lagrangian mechanics action problem. Because length is parameter-independent, we choose an affine parameterization such that \(g_{ab} T^a T^b = 1\). The variation \(\delta l\) is:

\[\begin{aligned} 0 &= \int_a^b \sum_{\alpha, \beta} \left\{ g_{\alpha \beta} \frac{dx^\alpha}{dt} \frac{d(\delta x^\beta)}{dt} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\sigma} \frac{\partial g_{\alpha \beta}}{\partial x^\sigma} \frac{dx^\alpha}{dt} \frac{dx^\beta}{dt} \delta x^\sigma \right\} dt \\ &= \int_a^b \sum_{\alpha, \beta} \left\{ - \frac{d}{dt} \left( g_{\alpha \beta} \frac{dx^\alpha}{dt} \right) + \frac{1}{2} \sum_\lambda \frac{\partial g_{\alpha \lambda}}{\partial x^\beta} \frac{dx^\alpha}{dt} \frac{dx^\lambda}{dt} \right\} \delta x^\beta dt \end{aligned}\]

For this integral to vanish for arbitrary variations \(\delta x^\beta\), the integrand must evaluate to zero:

\[- \sum_\alpha g_{\alpha \beta} \frac{d^2 x^\alpha}{dt^2} - \sum_{\alpha, \lambda} \frac{\partial g_{\alpha \beta}}{\partial x^\lambda} \frac{dx^\lambda}{dt} \frac{dx^\alpha}{dt} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\alpha, \lambda} \frac{\partial g_{\alpha \lambda}}{\partial x^\beta} \frac{dx^\alpha}{dt} \frac{dx^\lambda}{dt} = 0\]

By isolating the second derivative and comparing it to the standard definition of the Christoffel symbols, this perfectly reproduces the geodesic equation. Thus, a curve extremizes length (or proper time) if and only if it is a geodesic.

(Note: While geodesics extremize length, they are not guaranteed to be the global minimum. Two points on a sphere's equator can be connected by two distinct geodesics, only one of which represents the shortest path.)

docs.title: 5. The Geodesic Deviation Equation
docs.text:
Finally, we establish the physical manifestation of curvature by analyzing how families of geodesics behave relative to one another.

Let \(\gamma_s (t)\) denote a smooth one-parameter family of geodesics. For each \(s \in \mathbb{R}\), \(\gamma_s\) is a geodesic parameterized by affine parameter \(t\). The mapping \((t,s) \mapsto \gamma_s (t)\) defines a two-dimensional submanifold \(\Sigma\). Because these are geodesics, their tangent vectors \(T^a = (\partial/\partial t)^a\) satisfy \(T^a abla_a T^b = 0\).

We define the deviation vector \(X^a = (\partial / \partial s)^a\), which represents the spatial displacement to an infinitesimally nearby geodesic. Because \(X^a\) and \(T^a\) are coordinate basis vectors of \(\Sigma\), they commute:

\[T^b abla_b X^a = X^b abla_b T^a\]

By utilizing gauge freedom in the affine parameterization, we can enforce \(X^a T_a = 0\) everywhere on \(\Sigma\).

The quantity \(v^a = T^b abla_b X^a\) describes the relative velocity of the nearby geodesic. Taking one more derivative gives the relative acceleration \(a^a = T^c abla_c v^a\). We can directly relate this acceleration to the Riemann tensor:

\[ egin{aligned} a^a &= T^c abla_c (T^b abla_b X^a) \\ &= T^c abla_c (X^b abla_b T^a) \\ &= (T^c abla_c X^b)( abla_b T^a) + X^b T^c abla_c abla_b T^a \\ &= (X^c abla_c T^b)( abla_b T^a) + X^b T^c abla_b abla_c T^a - R_{cbd}{}^a X^b T^c T^d \\ &= X^c abla_c (T^b abla_b T^a) - R_{cbd}{}^a X^b T^c T^d \\ &= - R_{cbd}{}^a X^b T^c T^d \end{aligned}\]

This result is the celebrated geodesic deviation equation. It definitively proves that \(a^a = 0\) for all families of geodesics if and only if the Riemann curvature tensor vanishes (\(R_{abc}{}^d = 0\)). In other words, tidal forces—the convergence or divergence of initially parallel free-falling test particles—are the strict geometric consequence of a non-zero Riemann tensor.
